cues.text: MIT 8107, Software Development Lifecycle.
Study Session 4: Agile Frameworks, Iterative and Incremental Development.
Chapter one: Agile principles.
Let's begin with the big idea.
Agile is a mindset.
It is not a single tool or a single document; it is a way of thinking about how software should be built.
Specifically, it is a mindset for adaptive value delivery.
Let me unpack that phrase.
"Adaptive" means the team expects to adjust as it learns.
"Value delivery" means the goal is to put something genuinely useful in front of the people who need it.
And the source tells us how this is achieved: through feedback, collaboration and technical discipline.
Those three ideas will keep coming back, so hold on to them.
Feedback tells the team whether it is on the right track.
Collaboration brings the right people together.
And technical discipline keeps the software sound while everything is changing.
Now, the foundation of Agile is the Agile Manifesto, and the Manifesto is built around four values.
It values people and interactions, working software, customer collaboration, and responding to change.
But notice the wording carefully: it values these more than their counterparts.
So each value is set against something else.
People and interactions are valued more than processes and tools.
Working software is valued more than comprehensive documentation.
Customer collaboration is valued more than contract negotiation.
And responding to change is valued more than following a plan.
Here is the qualification that students often miss.
The word is "more than", not "instead of".
The source states plainly that the Manifesto retains necessary tools, documentation, contracts and plans.
So Agile does not throw those things away.
A team still uses tools, still writes the documentation it needs, still works under contracts, and still makes plans.
The point is about emphasis: when there is tension, the first-named value gets the priority.
Next come the twelve principles.
The source gives them in paraphrased form, so I will take them in order.
First: satisfy customers through early and continuous delivery of valuable software.
Notice both words, early and continuous.
Value should arrive soon, and keep arriving.
Second: welcome changing requirements.
Change is not treated as a nuisance to be resisted; it is welcomed.
Third: deliver working software frequently.
Short intervals between releases mean more chances for feedback.
Fourth: business people and developers collaborate daily.
They do not work in separate worlds and meet only at handovers.
Fifth: build projects around motivated individuals.
The idea is to have people who are motivated to do the work.
Sixth: communicate effectively.
The source adds a note here: the original wording emphasises face-to-face communication.
So the paraphrase says "effectively", but the original stresses talking face to face.
Seventh: working software is the primary measure of progress.
Not the volume of documents, but software that actually works.
Eighth: maintain a sustainable pace.
Teams should be able to keep going steadily, rather than burning out.
Ninth: give continuous attention to technical excellence and good design.
This is where technical discipline, which we mentioned at the start, shows up directly in the principles.
Tenth: simplicity, which means avoiding unnecessary work.
Eleventh: self-organising, or self-managing, teams generate good solutions.
The team itself decides how to organise its work.
And twelfth: regularly reflect and adapt.
The team periodically steps back, considers how it is working, and adjusts accordingly.
Let me read those twelve once more as a compact list, so you can memorise them.
Early continuous valuable delivery.
Welcoming changing requirements.
Frequent working software.
Daily business and developer collaboration.
Motivated individuals.
Effective communication, with the original emphasising face-to-face.
Working software as the primary progress measure.
Sustainable pace.
Technical excellence and good design.
Simplicity and avoiding unnecessary work.
Self-organising, self-managing teams.
And regular reflection and adaptation.
Finally, there is one closing warning in the source, and it is important.
Agile is not the absence of planning, documentation or accountability.
A common misunderstanding is that "being Agile" means no plans, no paperwork and no one answerable for anything.
That is wrong.
Agile teams plan, they document what is necessary, and they remain accountable.
What changes is how and when these things are done, and how readily they are adjusted as feedback arrives.

So, to bring it together: Agile is a mindset of adaptive value delivery, expressed through four Manifesto values, twelve principles, and a firm understanding that it never means abandoning planning, documentation or accountability.
